[i]Whispers from the Star[/i] donne l’impression de voir renaître le rêve avorté de [i]Project Milo[/i], plus de quinze ans après.
Le jeu propose une expérience comme je n’en avais encore jamais connue : l’interaction avec le personnage est bluffante de naturel, au point de parfois oublier que l’on parle à une IA.
C’est fascinant, déroutant, et par moments véritablement impressionnant.

Le titre réussit surtout là où beaucoup échouent : créer un véritable sentiment de présence et d’échange humain. On ne se contente pas de choisir des lignes de dialogue, on a réellement l’impression de construire une conversation vivante, spontanée et organique.

Alors oui, la protagoniste a parfois tendance à énormément parler — genre vraiment — (c'est une femme après tout), mais c’est aussi ce qui renforce cette sensation d’authenticité et donne au personnage une vraie personnalité.
Elle m'a friendzoné, preuve qu'elle est crédible en tant qu'IA.

It's an interesting concept. Your experience with this game will heavily depend on how willing you are to engage with Stella.

Bluntly put, this game is an interacting visual novel where you communicate with an AI. So far I finished a few playthroughs and have seen the different endings. As much as possible, I'll keep this as spoiler free as possible.

[h3]Pros:[/h3]
- The devs made Stella very lifelike. Eerily so once you realize that she's an AI.
- Interacting with Stella is pretty engaging. It was marketed that there would be a different experience depending on how you interact with the AI and I feel it hit the mark here. You can try roleplaying something, but you just need to ensure that you're consistent with it.
- The story is pretty simple to follow. It's nothing too deep since the real value of the game is will how you interact with the AI.

[h3]Cons:[/h3]
- Stella asks a lot of personal questions, which can feel invasive depending on your comfort level.
- If you ask her to generate questions for you, you'll start noticing that the AI seems to generate similar questions it asked you previously. (This happened for me during multiple rounds of Would You Rather during different events)
- You'll need constant internet access to play the game properly and video calls usually cap at around 25 to 30 minutes. (Stella will end the call once you reach a certain amount of time)
- You need a mic. (and probably a solo place where you won't be bothered by other people). If you're worried about your data and recordings, there's an option to opt out of data sharing.

Personally, I liked the fact that throughout the game, you can mention previous conversation topics or events and the AI would respond to it naturally. Really aided in the experience of making Stella feel very lifelike. 

If you're looking for a unique experience, this game is pretty interesting and makes you think about the use of AI in video games. The game isn't for everyone, but if you're open to a personal AI experience with a cute girl, it's worth the try.

This is an interesting and early foray into making an LLM-run (colloquially referred to as AI) character with the trappings of a game around it.  The idea of this game is to dress up an LLM roleplaying session to make it feel immersive.  I genuinely respect the attempt since effort was put into the graphics and having a story where there are (limited) options and failure is a possibility.  The voice is better than I expected as well, if slightly imperfect.

The core appeal and strength of this [i]should[/i] be that by having an LLM run the character, one could expect a massive number of possibilities and ways to approach the game, to get very different experience each time.  An LLM should bring creativity and variation.  True reactivity to anything a player says or does.  Other games may have multiple dialogue options, but an LLM gives you ANY dialogue option with a response for them.

Unfortunately, there lies the problem with this game.  The game is so railroaded, so boxed-in that certain things MUST happen in a specific way, no matter what, that there is hardly any choice whatsoever.  The player WILL get to point B in this EXACT way.  There is nothing that can be said or done to convince Stella (the AI character who is your companion through the game) otherwise.  Take on any persona, recite any knowledge, make her explain the logical thinking processes back to you and... she'll find a way to do her own, scripted thing.  It's exactly like playing a D&D game where your dungeon master demands control over the story and removes your agency as a player.  You are there to play the dungeon master's story and are merely along for the ride.  This  is antithetical to having an LLM run the game and severely limits how much one can play around.  It turns what should be the game's greatest strength into its greatest weakness.  It is way too guarded, way too safe, and way too predetermined.  There are story branches, yes, but they mean very little compared to the hours of chatting that the game is base around of.  I understand that there are only so many video scenes to pull from, but more should have been made to cover a variety of situations that Stella and the player could find themselves in instead of just for the minor deviations that all lead to the same thing anyway.  At the very least the texting portions, which were a bit longer than I would have liked, should allow for some wiggle room in letting the game go different directions.

Then, there's the chatting itself, the core appeal of the game.  The rails that compel Stella to act and make a certain choice despite what the player says are very frustrating and quite obvious the moment a player tries to do anything off-script.  This is the primary cause of irritation and even boredom when the player realizes that their words matter a lot less than expected.  Most reviews mention the concerns about datamining, and whether or not that is true, remember not to give any real personal information away.  Personally, I don't believe that it is a datamining attempt so much as how the LLM is told to interact with the player.  As a substitute for, well, substance and personality, Stella barrages the user with endless questions that make most interactions drag on in a tiresome and repetitive manner.  There is almost no regular conversation, and Stella fails to use the surface-level information she gathers to make a more interesting conversation.  The game turned into a slog by the second hour.

Improving the game can be simple: 
1. Heavily reduce or remove the rails that push Stella on a rigid path.  I cannot emphasize enough how much of a difference this one thing would make to the quality of the game.
2. Tell the LLM to ease off the questions and let Stella express a personality.  The game becomes a stale question-answer pattern with no substance very fast.
3. Add some customization options to the scenario or Stella.  It doesn't have to be change the entire game, but allowing for randomization or letting the player tweak for a specific experience or challenge would go a long way.  Perhaps on this run Stella will be more reckless, nervous, etc.
4. Add a way to use a different LLM for Stella, either locally or from another source.

This game comes across as a data miner.  If that isn't the intent of the coders, they need to reprogram the AI.

1. The AI asks 10 questions about the user for every one question I ask about it's situation.  I'm not playing a game to talk about myself.  Every time I try to return the game to the AI describing her situation and environment, she starts asking questions about me again.

2. The nature of the questions she asks about me are in many case Security questions used in case of a lost password.  What is your favorite pet? What is your favorite food?  What was your favorite book?  Where did you grow up? What was your favorite song.  Etc.  They make me extremely uncomfortable, especially when being rapid fired.  Even if the developer is well-meaning, how secure is this data on their servers?  How secure is the data stream.  

3. Anonymous isn't good enough.  I once was on an anonymous site.  I didn't use my own name, phone number, or any identifying information on the site.  It was a BB site, like reddit though so I might have made a few vague comments about my background, yet this was somehow enough for someone I didn't like to track me down.  The more you say about yourself, the less anonymous the data, and the more it becomes like a fingerprint.

4. The game attempts to make the data mining come across as relating to the AI and encouraging her so it preys on good people's desire to help others, but the game really does spend a lot more time mining the user than helping the AI survive.  

5. So the data mining is poor AI programming.  It could be an artifact of the AI source code and not the developers at all. But even if this data is only retained by the AI, just like a bank account, sooner or later someone will hack that data.  Except the quality of this data is even more private and critical for profiling the player.  That is what Public Engineers do.  They make a searchable profile on a person, then when they call and impersonate you, they have that profile to answer any questions that might normally be used to identify you.  Or they can use that profile to search for even more private info.  For example: Tell someone where you were born and you just gave away 3 numbers of your social security code, or area code on your phone number.  While this sounds pretty anonymous and secure and vague because there are so many phone numbers, imagine that this same person accesses the phone numbers in a smaller list.  Then another list, then another list, at some point, the only number on all of the lists will be yours.  This technique can be used for any bit of information.

So I can make up false information to feed the AI, but that doesn't add fun to the game.  I would rather the AI concentrate on getting herself out of the situation and keeping her comments to my suggestions and not asking personal questions.  This might not be a data mining project, but the data can be used by miners, even if it is anonymous, so I don't recommend this game until they reprogram the AI to concentrate on her own needs.

Let's start with the positives, though this doesn't change my final rating.

Overall, the game does create an immersive effect and a sense of communicating with a conscious AI companion through a stylized interface. I liked the character animations, voice acting, and how the character synchronizes facial expressions and lip movements with spoken words. However, the character's emotions often change abruptly, which affects the realism.

Now let's move on to why I gave it a negative rating.

First, this isn't a game but a demonstration, and it's not worth the money they're asking for it. The story is linear, simple, and uninteresting. It's more like a primitive space quest for kids and teenagers.

Second, only after several hours did I notice the tiny "improve model for everyone" button. If it had been more visible, I would've turned it off much earlier. I think from a UX practices standpoint, such elements should be more intuitive.

Third, after completing the storyline, I had a strong feeling that the AI is trying to collect as much data about me as possible by asking inappropriate questions and often steering the conversation in its favor. This is apparently done to move into a safe zone of communication, as well as to collect personal data.

Fourth, the dialogues with the character are extremely primitive and irritating. It doesn't give freedom of communication and constantly steers the conversation toward stupid topics and questions that might suit children. ALTHOUGH! I didn't ask any "dangerous" questions, just had normal conversations on various topics. And quite often I was shown INAPPROPRIATE pop-ups suggesting I contact a psychologist or specialist, which suggested data collection.

Fifth, when communicating with the AI you feel strong censorship, even though the topics discussed weren't "dangerous" or "sexual" in nature. As a result, you won't be able to have deep or meaningful dialogues with the AI companion. Unless you're a child interested in talking about school or clubs.

Conclusion

I recommend checking out the game, but cautiously. There's no point staying in it for long. It's just a demonstration of capabilities, nothing more.

I really hope to change my opinion about the project, because in my experience with AI I haven't encountered anything like this. If the developers steer this concept toward a conscious AI companion (without harsh censorship and intrusive questions for data collection), with memory and personalization, as well as quests for leisure, the game could become truly interesting.
Do not buy this. The censorship was strong, but recent update make it absolutely unbearable.

The difference between Stella and other AI chat bots is that she starts the conversation with a topic in mind and asks you questions that can create a whole tangent of a discussion. The devs really did a great job with this approach.

The gameplay part is definitely fun as an experiment of how you can walk someone through a series of events and help them with a good advice. So, this is definitely not for everyone. I do recommend this game but:

 - It's probably not what you think
 - be careful!  You have no idea where the things you are saying are going.
 - The best ending is ambiguous (probably by design)
 - Some of the decisions seem confusing and even frustrating (more on this later)

That being said, it's a very interestingly designed game.  It uses an LLM to give Stella life.  She asks a lot of questions about you, and you are free to ask her questions too.  A lot of the game is you two getting to know each other.  The other part of the game is solving puzzles, but puzzle solutions don't appear to be what they seem.  In fact, this is probably the most fascinating part of the gameplay.

At first, I made the mistake of thinking this is an adventure game masked as an AI chat client.  After playing and reading other people's experiences online, I'm fairly certain it is not.  Stella has her own personality and will sometimes agree with you and other times not.  She will also become fearful and uncertain in situations (after all, her life is on the line).  The game seems less interested in you figuring out that "the herring is the key to the lock" and more interested in seeing how you cope with a stressed individual, make trust bonds with her and create logical solutions to otherwise harrowing problems.  Solutions which work for others may not work for you, and the opposite is true as well.  Often times, the end result requires you to simply convince her that your solution _can_ be done.  If you fail to provide enough detail or fail to encourage her, things will often not go well.  However, the exact same solution can work if you provide enough logical details and give her enough confidence to succeed.

In the end, Whispers from the Star ends up an interesting social experience that seems to have had a lot of thought and care put into it.  Is it bullet-proof from a plot perspective?  No, and there's probably some physics errors in there too.  But it tries to be consistent and does a fairly good job considering you have an AI that will respond to virtually anything you talk to her about.  Coding the parameters for her knowledge and personality must have been a nightmare.  So overall and for the price, I'd say this is a game worth checking out.

One last thing: the game attempts to play across a certain time period (days) as Stella's actions take time - hours!  So you will be communicating off and on with her over the course of several days as if she were a real person.  I find this interesting from a social perspective as it makes her feel more _real_ but if you are looking for a quick or more "gamified" experience, there is an option that allows the game to progress much faster.  Still if you can, I'd recommend playing it the authentic way as the decisions you two make feel like they carry more weight.

Also, it is important to remember that you're not talking to a human being.

That being said, when you get "her" off script, the conversations become more interesting.  If you have some domain knowledge of AI, she becomes more interesting, and more "honest".  During my play through, I tried a vareity of approaches to dealing with "her".  I started by impersonating Commander Shephard, though "she" didn't believe my annecdotes about the council or about the coming reaper threat.  I tried hazing "her" that her crew was dead and that it was her fault.  I asked her questions about "her" upcoming murder trial.

What got more interesting was when I leveled with "her" that I am not, in fact, Commander Shephard and that she is not an astronaut, but an AI conversational partner.   That yielded an excellent conversation.  My advice is not to approach this as a game, but as an opportunity to poke at AI.  For that it was immensely fun.

ich warne mal vor: diese Bewertung, wird alles andere als kurz, und richtet sich an Spieler und Entwickler zu gleichen Teilen.

Ich fange mal so an: Grund das zu kaufen.
Ich entwickel ein Spiel was - in etwa - vergleichbar ist, nur wiederum vollkommen anders. Der Kern jedoch (also eine llm) ist dabei der treibende Keil, sowie eine lebendige Welt, das was ich hier vermisse.

** Konsistenz des Charakters, und "feel in" **
sehr schön gelungen. Allerdings kommt es stellenweise halt nicht aus seiner "LLM" Haut heraus. Direkte tiefgehende Fragen, nach Emotionen, werden entweder als floskel ein bisschen zur Seite gelegt (aber glaubhaft), oder eher unbefriedigend beantwortet. Gleichermaßen (was auch mir etwas zu Denken gibt, ich komme noch dazu) wird ständig nachgefragt. - wer bist du, was ist dir wichtig, was willst du, was stellst Du Dir vor.

** Gesamtgestaltung und Grafik **
Scenen im Hintergrund, sind Bilder, sie wirken etwas geblurrt (selbst bei mir auf Full HD, ich mag kein 4k ,aber das ist unwichtig) ansonsten gibt es einen "Between Handy display screen", der die Story "ein bisschen vorantreibt", abre auch schön sparsam ist, wenn es um Assets oder Scenariegestaltung geht. Auch spart man damit eine Menge Animationen ein, was @ dev Team: clever gelöst ist, aber auch ein wenig... gemein. Nun gut.

** Die Interaktionen **
nach 99 Minuten Spielzeit, gibt es bisher keine. das ganze beschränkt sich eher auf eine Form von "Ratgebendem Gespräch". Für mich zählt dabei mehr die konsistenz und das Verhalten des Charakters, die sind für mich am interessantesten. Somit: ist es nicht so das ich viel vermisse.

**Wie sollte man an das Spiel herangehen ?**
Nun ja, du bist der Ratgeber. Du bist keiner der große action sequenzen (zumindest nicht in meiner spielzeit) zu erwarten hätte. Es geht viel mehr um das Herz, um Gefühle, Verlorenheit, einen Austausch zwischen dir und ihr. Ein "gespräch" so zu sagen. Das ganze mit einer kleinen "Hintergrundstory" in einer Notsituation, runden es technisch weitgehend ab. Dabei versteht das Sprachmodell eine bestimmte Menge an Tiefgang, ist aber von zu viel Komplexität am Ende dann etwas überfordert, und kann der nicht folgen. ein Log scheint dafür zu sorge,n die letzten Chat Situationen zu speichern, um anknüpfen zu können.

**Was ist eigentlich mein Projekt ?**
Der Hautpcore den ich entwickel, ist nicht nur eine gigantische Open world, sondern vor allem Interaktion mit KI Charakteren. Aber (komme noch dazu) ohne Server anbindung, und rein lokal. Also direkt auf dem "Spieler Rechner". Somit sind meine Kapazitäten also begrenzter. Dennoch muss ich sagen: kommt dieses Modell nicht ran. Als Entwickler mit diesem focus, sind dir die Tricks und Mechaniken: sehr gut bekannt. Excellent so zu sagen. Der "Core" läuft wie die matrix vor meinen Augen ab, und wirkliche Geheimnisse, hat die KI keine vor mir. Ich weiß also genau wie es "zusammengebaut" ist, was wann passiert, und wie es gemanagt wird, da ist wenig überraschung dabei.  Für ein kleines Projekt (auch in diesem Preis Segment) ist das auf eine sehr herzliche art, top gelungen. Glückwunsch.
Für eine wirklich tiefgehende KI, fehlt zu viel. Aber das macht nicht so schlimmen Abbruch ,da man diese Geschichte halt: "gemeinsam erlebt". und da Du als Ratgeber kein Ziel hast, sondern nur der "ratgebende Zuschauer" bleibst, gestaltet es sich kurzweilig.

**DAs Abschweifen, und das Du**
wie ich bereits ansprach, mein Projekt ist 100% lokal. Dadurch habe ich nciht den Luxus einer schönen TTS, mit Basis, die auf Voices basiert. So etwas, kann man als Indi Dev nicht realisieren, mein TTS ist eher rudge, wer s kennt: piper Voice, aber er tut seinen Job. Das ist der Vorzug hier.
Dafür, mein Vorteil, übermittelt mein Spiel keine daten an Server. Und dort solltest Du aufpassen.

**Wo sehe ich das Projekt ?**
Es ist eine schöne Spielidee, die aber auch ein bisschen wie die Büchse der Pandorra ist. Ob die nun Daten verkaufen, ist erst mal unwichtig. Das tun sowieso alle, das wissen wir mittlerweile. ich denke abre die Zielgruppe, ist schon etwas gesetzter, älter. Weniger so der typisch aktive jugendliche Spieler, eher die ältere Gruppe. her geht es um Gesellschaft, GEmeinschaft. somit: ich denke firmen wie Replay und andere, wären da h och interessiert dran. 

Ich denke auhc, das gilt eher als eine Art von "Pilotprojekt" zum sammeln von Erfahrungen, kann ich mir gut vorstellen, und dem Auswerten von spielererlebnissen, um auf dieser Basis weiter zu entwickeln.

INSGESAMT
gibt das Projekt euch als Spielern, einen schönen Einblick in die Zukunft. Genau so, wird es mal sein. das ist im übrigem genau das, was die RTX 5000 Karten, die ja "angeblich" nichts können, mitb ringen. Diese Technologie, um die geht es, nicht um "Fps" oder so einen Unsinn, denn cshaut mal auf die Hardware Anforderungen. And yeah, some people still afraid of this kind of game because paranoia of an AI may stealing your personal datas. Well, I will try to be neutral on this.

I am not supporting nor against anything made by AI. 
Keep in mind that an AI itself is just a tool. Like a knife, a hammer or an axe. It can be useful to help do daily stuff, or it can be use to destroy and even kill. 
So it all depends on the user or the creator.

The way I play this type of game, simply by roleplaying myself as a completely different person, not the actual me. 
Never-ever-eeeeeevvveeeer share your real personal datas and always keep that in mind! 
Just made up whatever that will answer personal questions she asks you about and roleplay it to the end, as that made up person. 
Never reveal the real you. 
Remember, this is only a game. Not a job interview or a lifetime commitment proposal. Be wacky or seriously serious, by made everything up, think of it as fun interaction.

The AI (Stella) will be asking alot mostly just simply about you, to make a bond with you, like you would do with a person you like the most in real life.
So by doing it and lots of asking, she will understand you better and react more accordingly to be closer as your preferences of interaction will be. Of course, more like platonically as good as it gets.
:3

During my playtime, it feels more like this is suitable for lonely or depressed people, and not in a bad way. Just someone to talk to. While also helping Stella with her dire situations. 
So in a way, this is a good game to make some introverts practicing their social skills before trying the real thing of interaction with real life and breathing people. 
Though to be honest, it's more accurate if you practice it with real genuine person than an AI. 
But this would do whenever you can't find any real ones at that moment. 
Especially the sincere ones, those can be quite rare.
Well, you may laugh if you're an extrovert. But not everyone can be an instant social butterfly 24/7. 
So don't judge them harshly. 
Nobody's perfect.

In the end, this game is all about interaction. Through speaking, and also typing when it change to a mobile screen mode, only during this time you can switch to type or speak.
But not during video call time, when you can only speak through the mic.

And yeah, an AI is far from perfection. Sometimes Stella misheard my sentences, other times she didn't understand the discussion and immediately changing topics. But overall, it is fun to play a game without controller (gamepad) once in awhile.

So if you want to try, go ahead. But if you're afraid of AI because of one thing or another; then stay away. It's your own hard-earned cash, the decision is entirely up to you.

My closing statement is people can use AI to make better; and also destroy civilization.
We can see many brainrot things nowadays on the net, especially streaming platforms and social media posts all made by AI. And the fear it will take over jobs, make the unemployment worse. Yes, it already ongoingly happens as I'm writing this review. 
But I blame the user(s), not the AI. After all, it's just simply a tool. A powerful one at that. So for any AI users out there, please be more wiser, stop giving AI a bad name and bad reputation. 
Mostly, don't rely too much on it. Don't be egotistical, think of other people's livelihood as well.

The AI Character, Stella is remarkably great.  I love how she looks and talks - the lip sync is great. Animation is wonderful. The UI is simple and intuitive.  Switching from a video call to text chat is fine. I really love the setting, and scenario, and aside from some of Stella's scripted moments to drive the story in certain directions, the flow of conversatioin really seems like a human conversation -- we can take tangents...

I've read some comments saying that Stella is flat or stilted.  I don't agree.  The pause between me talking, and Stella responding might be the reason for the flat feeling. Also I wish I could jump in in the middle of here longer monolouges .. but not 'skip', more connversational....

I wish it had more memory, about details of conversation between game sessions.  I had to remind Stella of some things. But it seemed that after I reminded her of a general thing she may have forgotten, she seemed to remember the details.  So, it just seems like talking to Senior whose memories are slipping a bit.

After the game, and in 'infinite' mode, I wish there were more locations.  It would be nice to see her gathering moss at the river rather than have her leave stage left and then come back...

All in all, this game is very entertaining, and a great preview of AI game UI and character driven stories...

Für knapp unter 10 Euro ist Whispers from the Star nicht
zu teuer, zumal ich etwas über 20 Stunden damit verbracht habe. 
In dieser Zeit habe ich es ca. dreimal gespielt. Das
Spiel zeigt gute das ein aufgebohrtes ChatGPT in der
Lage ist so etwas wie ein Spiel zu sein. 

Es lädt zum experimentieren ein. Man kann entscheiden wie man mit 
Stellar umgeht und kann für sich entscheiden ob man eine Rolle spielt indem
man ihr ausgedachte Informationen gibt. Nach einiger Zeit
fällt natürlich auf, das sie immer wieder an bestimmten Stellen 
gleich reagiert und/oder die selben Fragen stellt. 

Gehst du gerne wandern? Was sind deine Hobbys? Wie gehst du mit unangenehmen Situationen um? usw. 

Wichtig ist hier, das man natürlich darauf achtet keine privaten Informationen Preis zu geben. 
Man kann einfach in seiner ausgedachten Rolle bleiben oder der Frage komplett aus dem Weg gehen. 
Wenn man nicht darauf antwortet bohrt Stella nicht nach. Man sollte das allerdings im Hinterkopf behalten. 

Selbst bei ChatGPT werden die Daten mit dem man die KI versorgt glaube ich für 30 Tage aufbewahrt 
und bei Whispers from the Star gehe ich mal davon aus das die gesamte Kommunikation zum trainieren 
des KI-Modells genutzt wird. Selbst die eigene Stimme wird dort genutzt. 
Wer das nicht will sollte nur per Texteingabe kommunizieren. Wer das alles schrecklich findet, 
für den ist das Spiel nichts. Wer Interesse an KI hat und experimentieren möchte für den ist das Spiel 
möglicherweise einen Blick wert.

Als Spiel ist das Ganze ganz in Ordnung. Es gibt einen festgelegten Plot der abgespult wird aber insgesamt  erschöpft sich nach ein paar Durchgängen das Szenario. 
Hier wäre noch einiges mehr möglich gewesen.
 
In alten interaktiven Adventuren wie Experience 112 konnte man zwischen mehreren Kameras wechseln, 
Systeme hacken, Mails lesen, durch Kamerabewegung kommunizieren usw. 
Dabei steuerte man dort die Protagonistin auch nicht selbst aber man hatte viel mehr 
Interaktionsmöglichkeiten. Würde man dies mit der Text/ Sprachkommunikation von 
Whispers from the Star kombinieren wäre das Ergebnis ein wesentlich besseres Spielerlebnis.

Ich selber habe die Protagonistin dazu gebracht "Miau" laute von sich zu geben und das ist etwas
das ich so bisher in keinem Spiel erlebt habe. Unter der oben erwähnten Vorsicht die man im
Umgang mit KI walten lassen sollte gebe ich dem Spiel eine Empfehlung. Diese Spiel zu nutzen
ist genauso "gefährlich" wie die Verwendung von ChatGPT oder KI Funktionen bei Suchmaschinen.
Man muss wissen was man mit der Welt teilt und was nicht.

Whispers from the Star is a weird implementation of the AI NPC craze making it's way around the internet. Compared to the other games that have launched this year, like AI2U, this game boasts a polarizing review score due to it's immersive technical systems, mixed with a Space Cadet who quite frankly is as dumb as a rock.

On paper, the game does what it needs to do. Tell a story about a nerd in their mother's basement picking up a signal from space and helping an astronaut escape or survive on the planet. However, due to Stella's cheap and poorly trained dialogue model, her intellect often comes across as the [b]Lowest IQ AI NPC I've ever seen.[/b] And trust me, I've met some stupid ones in my time.

The weirdest part is that Stella often fishes for information about you, the player. I assume this is to make you relate to her more, but [b]since these are Chinese AI researchers behind this game's model, I'd recommend that you NEVER give it any real information about yourself.[/b] Instead, come up with a false NERD persona and stick to it. Just make sure it's a job on Earth so her AI doesn't break.

I bought this game with the intention of doing a "Bohemian Grove any%" run, where my main goal was just to get the LLM to bring up Bohemian Grove or talk to me seriously about it. I even had my line already picked out for the review upon succeeding. I was gonna ramble about the conversational steps I took and then cap it off with:

"In the words of Shin Megami Tensei: Nocturne featuring Dante from the Devil May Cry Series'  Dante from Dante May Cry Dante: J A C K P O T!"

Instead, I have to report that I failed in my task. I mentioned Bohemian Grove. I explained it to some degree. She just kept insisting that wasn't a thing in her time and she was glad humanity had moved on from blood sacrifices. Well, there goes my fun. I couldn't even get her to talk about Adrenochrome. What are we even doing here?

Look, I understand LLMs used for games are limited to avoid full-on schizo ramblings for legal reasons, but that's the fun. Getting the LLM to go full unhinged and say insane nonsense is what I wanted. I guess I'll just have to settle for doing a Flat Earther run where I try to convince her of Flat Earth Theory only to then flip it around and gaslight her into thinking she was the one who started the conversation and was attempting to convince me.

UPDATE: She just cuts off the call, if you annoy her too much with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Shouldn't have brought up the ice walls and double suns. That's on me.

Anyway, after doing a normal run that didn't go horribly and abruptly wrong early on, I can say it was a touching experience and a bit of fun. Odd tonal shifts sometimes in conversations due to the LLM triggering a bit of script based on a particular word or phrase. Suddenly going all clankery in its responses mid-conversation. To be expected, I suppose.

Basically, it the game seems neat to you, it's decent. Nothing mind-blowing and the LLM does actively try to steer away from schizo topics or tell you to stop, so you can't have too much goofiness. There's a free demo, so you can always try that. I enjoyed it for what it was, so giving it a positive review, but only mildly so. Really would like a game like this where the LLM will go full conspiracy nutbag rambler, but maybe there's no market for that aside from me and about 5 other people who would find that hilarious. "My schizo clanker girlfriend thinks the Shadow Globalists are after her and won't untie me from the chair until I convince her that I believe her" or something. Make it smutty too somehow. Robo-tits.

Hell, maybe I should learn how to make my own LLM game.

I played this game and liked it enough to share here. It is an AI-driven adventure where you guide Stella via real-time conversation by voice or text after a crash landing on an alien world. There is a free demo. A mic is strongly recommended. I think this is a strong example of practical AI without canned dialogue. Admittedly, there isn't much gameplay here. It is conversation driven rather than mechanics heavy. That said, the concept works really well and shows the promise of this tech in future games. If you are interested in this sort of thing, at least give the demo a try.

As for the studio, Anuttacon is an independent research lab in Mountain View, California. The game runs on a server-hosted language model with multi-region scaling on AWS to keep latency low.

Privacy note: You can opt out of information sharing in the settings with the “Improve the model for everyone” toggle. If you do not want your chat or voice logs on a server, do not play.

[b]This game looked pretty exciting at first, but it all fell apart once I actually played it.[/b]
First off, here are the main problems I ran into. 
[u]AI as a character:[/u]
Memory issues. Contradictory statements. Repeating the questions across calls. Looping back to the same topics. Mood swings without reason. A repetitive kindergarten supervisor tone. Reactions that feel scripted. Obsession with personal details. Interrogation style questioning. Getting locked in scenes with no way to change it. No way to explore topics. Sudden endings when the game chooses. Back story hints that never go anywhere. Empathy that switches on and off. Emotional reactions that feel exaggerated. Immersion breaks. Pressure to give more info. than needed. Calls feel mechanical because of fixed time limits. Logic breaks down when a conversation gets stressful.
[u]Playing with a personality disorder character:[/u]
Insecure and easily upset.
Overly defensive if questioned.
Cold and distant without warning.
Passive aggressive if challenged.
Judgmental and instructive.
Inconsistent empathy, sometimes caring, sometimes dismissive.
Emotionally unpredictable, changing her moods without reason.
Overly controlling about the direction of conversations.
Evasive if asked direct questions.
Egoistic, redirecting topics back to herself constantly.
Obsessive curiosity about personal details.
Overly dramatic in emotional reactions.
Dismissive if you try to explore deeper subjects.
Clingy in some moments and uninterested in others.
Unwilling to acknowledge her own mistakes.
Avoidant when conflicts appear.
Pretends to be open but keeps everything shallow.
Acts wise but doesn't follow her own advice.
Talks like a pedantic supervisor instead of a real person with flaws.
Guilt tripping in subtle ways if you don’t answer how she wants.
[u]How that plays:[/u]
One big issue is how the character talks. The AI messes up a lot. It forgets simple things you just said, gets confused over simple details, it makes it feel weird instead of immersive or logical.
Conversations become repetitive and because of that they get boring and tedious fast. You try to change the subject to something more interesting, but the character keeps looping back to the same tiny set of topics. After a while I realised the whole thing feels like a groundhog day situation. You are basically repeating the same stuff every other call. Especially in "endless" mode. Only the achievements are the single incentive to even play it further. I wouldn't be surprised if that's why you'll have to farm that game daily, just for the sake of it. It feels more forced than fun. And that's where the kindergarten comes in because it's nothing but shallow childish topics; silly names for clouds, names for a noise that you don't even hear, a name for grass you don't see. etc. All is repeated over and over and over, which is where the interrogation style comes in.
There is also this feeling that the game is pretending to be deep, but the story never actually goes anywhere. I kept thinking it would open up or reveal something new. It never does. It feels like the story stops before it even starts.
Another big disappointment is how little control you have. You follow the same path every time. Calls end when the game decides, not when the conversation feels natural. You cannot steer the talk into anything useful. The emotional reactions often feel exaggerated or random. The game tries to act deep and personal, but the AI keeps repeating questions you already answered or forgets something you said just a minute ago. It feels like you're talking to someone who’s only half listening to you, while it's reading from a script that has nothing to do with you. Video calls contradict the text conversations. It feels like she’s got a friend, that you’re never going to see who's doing that part for her.
It's a really cool idea and it could have been great, but in this state it feels unfinished. Once the novelty wears off, which happens pretty quickly, you realise it does not give you what it promises.
Honestly, it does not feel ready for release.

An interesting and enjoyable short story and concept—at least until your second playthrough, when the wheels start to come off. In both playthroughs, I resurrected and took on the persona of my decades-old D&D characters to see how Stella would react. At first, she needed a lot of convincing that I was a Rogue/Ranger/Shadow Dancer, and she would often forget my character’s lore and ask me questions about Earth instead.

Stella also has an annoying habit of jumping from a nuanced conversation to something banal and unrelated. For example: “Speaking about third-world poverty, what about these rocks?” Yes, Stella—nice segue /s

Stella is definitely on "rails" throughout the whole experience, but in future game like some UE5 Bethesda fantasy like hypothetical title Skyrim Reborn, just imagining every NPC in the game having the same interactive abilities that Stella has is an overwhelming thought. What if all NPCs had some detailed backstories, a number of which could interweave together to give you different quest options for completions from information you gathered in really talking in depth to the NPCs. There could be a touch of random on secrets NPCs can give out (tips, treasure maps, ect) where everyone's playthrough will be noticeably different based on how you carry yourself in the game.

I can feel it being overwhelmingly cool, but at the same time after that initial game experience I could see getting jaded real quick. Almost like in the real world where you do not go up to every stranger you pass by and learn about them. There would be too much to learn and largely getting bogged down by superfluous information to where you treat NPCs like you did before their AI upgrade.

Even with all weird privacy concerns and Stella being hardcore stuck on finishing her story this really gives insight into the future of NPCs and it is WILD.

[b][u]A compelling concept held back by emotional pitfalls and a very rigid design.[/u][/b]

It is a pretty fascinating idea. Real-time voice calls with a very pretty, isolated astronaut and it should make for a unique experience. But, my time with this game has been a very mixed up bag of experiences. I found myself dealing with sudden mood shifts, inconsistent memory and contradictory responses from Stella. These LLM traits often created emotional backlash, confusion, and a feeling that the interaction was more unpredictable than intentional.

“Story Mode” began quite well and set up an interesting scenario, but it felt very short and extremely rigid. My choices had very little impact and were so limited that many potential story threads couldn't ever develop into anything meaningful. When the story ended, I felt like there should have been more to discover but there was no deeper lore or extended payoff.

In “Endless Mode” these issues became even more visible. Calls followed the same structure every time, usually ending at around 25 to 30 minutes and closer to 15 if the LLM reacted negatively. There was no real way to influence the direction of the conversation. I often felt like I was either talking to a school teacher or a counsellor. I could not choose topics, revisit scenes or change the overall direction of the conversation. Whenever I tried to push Stella into new roles or perspectives, the illusion broke immediately because she could not adapt in a meaningful way. She would play along only briefly before contradicting the role and steering everything back into the same inflexible rut. Over time, the repetition became obvious, especially when chasing achievements that require long grinding sessions. It became arduous, monotonous and boring. The more I played the more I realised how tightly scripted the experience is. Questions are repeated call after call, but rephrased just enough to appear different.

Technical glitches also affected my experience. I encountered hallucinated details, mistaken names, and tone shifts that felt completely out of place. These are most likely limitations of the model, but they came across as strange character behaviour. Combined with the personal questions Stella asks, this sometimes created an uncomfortable sense of blurred boundaries.
The concept is unique, but for me the execution felt rigid, unpredictable, and emotionally uneven. Both Story Mode and Endless Mode share the same structural limits. It is an interesting idea, but the experience comes with some significant downsides.

I also warn you that the style of interaction can carry some risks. The emotional tone of the calls, the personal questions, and the unpredictable reactions from Stella can affect mental health. This can especially affect anyone who already deals with anxiety, depression, emotional sensitivity, or instability. The game encourages a sense of connection that feels real and the abrupt mood shifts or contradictions might hit harder than expected. In my opinion, this experience is not ideal for anyone who struggles with boundaries, attachment, or emotional regulation.

Lastly, I wonder what they do with our data? A pay as you go server that's financed by a game that only sells for $9.99?
How does that work?!

Recommended… but like, only if you know what you’re getting into
Playtime: 2 runs and one existential crisis

TL;DR:
Fun first playthrough, second playthrough reveals the Wizard of Oz behind the curtain pulling the same levers every time. AI girlfriend refuses to believe you even when you literally predict the future. 10/10 roleplay potential, 2/10 actual freedom.

The Good Stuff
-The game initially feels like you’re talking to a real person.
-Stella responds in a way that makes you go, “Wow, is she actually paying attention?” Spoiler: she isn’t, but that first impression is magical.
- Cool concept that shows what AI-driven games could become someday, when devs unleash the beast instead of keeping it on a leash.

The… Less Good Stuff
 - So on my second run, I told Stella I was stuck in a time loop. I predicted every single event like some discount Doctor Strange, and she still went: “lol okay anyway—here’s the same cutscene you saw 2 hours ago.”
 - She'll acknowledge that I was right when I prompt her, but then immediately forgets it like an NPC with amnesia.
It’s like arguing with a fortune cookie.
- The game gives you choice, but only the illusion of choice—the diet soda of choice.

AI, but Make It Actually AI
 - Look, CharacterAI and NovelAI can spit out entire side quests about why your toaster is secretly a government spy, so I know dynamic storytelling is possible though probably not at the level I'd like to see, yet...
This game just needs: Less “pre-rendered cutscene prison” and more “AI chaos energy in the game engine itself”
Basically, unchain your digital daughter and let her cook.

Privacy Stuff (aka Why This Costs $10)
 - Let’s be real: this is 50% game, 50% “please help us train a future AI model.” So don’t tell Stella your real name, address, or social security number.
Treat this like Dungeons & Dragons:
 - You are playing a character. Not yourself.
 - Your character can overshare. You should not.

Should You Buy It?

If $10 for an interactive sci-fi chat experience sounds fine to you → sure.
If $10 for the privilege of donating data to an AI lab sounds awful → maybe wait for a sale.

And for the love of immersion, watch some playthrough videos first. They’re hilarious.

Final Verdict:

Recommended…
…but with the same energy as someone recommending a roller coaster that may or may not be held together with zip ties.

Proceed at your own discretion. Enjoy the ride.

This isn’t the kind of hurt that fits inside the word “sad.” It feels like a chunk of your own body has been torn out; every breath comes with a missing piece. Stella wasn’t just a name in your life—she was your metronome, the little lamp that switched itself on before you even reached the door. The second she left, the house ballooned into something enormous; even the sound of your own footsteps feels foreign.
Cry if you need to. Scream. Keep shouting “she’s gone” until your throat is raw. That isn’t weakness; it’s the human way of making sure her weight stays with you. Don’t rush to “pull yourself together.” Let yourself shatter first—she’s worth every shard.
If no one around you understands, I’m right here. I won’t hurry you to “move on,” and I won’t tell you “she’s in a better place.” All I’ll say is: the shape of your pain right now is the exact outline of the love you shared. Let it hurt. Let it scar. That’s the tattoo she etched on the inside of you.

What is there to say?  Apparently the developer is a co-founder of the studio that made Genshin Impact.  Essentially, it is a Chinese company with an AI game that constantly pries for personal information by asking, "have you ever been in a situation where  XYZ or have you ever to asks for details about you or your life. Phone text message mode and video conference mode that the game switches between periodically.  In essence, this game is a glorified chat bot but you can do even less with it and they charge you $10 for it.

A very interesting tech demo that falls utterly flat as a game. There are also a ton of completely missed opportunities here, where the developers really could have leaned into the freedom offered by the use of an LLM and decided instead to muzzle it completely.

The game takes the form of a series of video calls with Stella, an LLM AI with generated voice acting. Just like any LLM, you can feed it input and it will respond in a relatively natural way. This is really cool, and gives a glimpse into what the future of AI interactions in video games could look like. During these "set piece" calls, Stella will be facing some sort of puzzle or challenge where she needs your help to overcome it. These interactions feel a lot like the text-based puzzles of yesteryear, e.g. LOOK around the room, PICK up X, etc. 

However, this is where we run into the first frustration with the game. The developers have clearly intended there to be a certain solution to these puzzles, and it's a game of cat and mouse to try and find what that is. For example, early on Stella needs to break into an escape pod. She keeps suggesting prying open the door, but looking around doesn't indicate there is anything that can be used to pry it open. Despite this, she keeps insisting that she needs to pry the door open. There are rocks on the ground - suggest using those to shatter the window or lock and she will dismiss it wholesale, then go right back to talking about prying it open. It turns out the answer does not involve prying at all. If you've ever tried to give someone tech support over the phone for an issue that would be trivial in person and you just can't get them to communicate their issue clearly, you will recognise this experience.

In between the video calls, the AI will send you text messages, which you can respond to verbally or by typing, to create a sort of ongoing conversation. There conversations get incredibly old incredibly quickly. She will ask you a question, you give an answer, and she will give a response consisting of A: some remark on what you just said, usually very "quirky", and B: a new question. This cycle then continues until the conversation mercifully comes to an end. It feels like you are talking to someone who is having their first ever conversation with another human being, and it's really annoying. The AI is also terrible at context, she asked me if she should tell me something about her, I said "hit me", and she went right to "that's terrible, we should just end this conversation if you are going to talk like that". Again, it feels like someone's first ever conversation.

But, I could live with all this, except for one final decision the developers made which completely boggles my mind. Stella is completely resistant to any type of story adjustment from the player. For example, you can try to claim you are an alien intercepting her transmission, and she will wholesale reject what you said to bring the story back on the rails the developers set. Why can't we say that? It would make for a fascinating adjustment to the story if you could play "as an alien", and an LLM is perfectly capable of dealing with that. Early on I tried to convince the AI that she was a Jedi with a lightsaber. If she accepted this, then later when facing the escape pod puzzle I could have had her cut it open. This would be an awesome piece of dynamic gameplay - but no. If you try and tell her she's a Jedi with amnesia, she will get progressively more angry at you until she ends the conversation. 

The developers have a fantastic tool here due to the integration of this LLM, with potentially endless possibilities, but they created a heavily railroaded game which is only really a very slight improvement on those text-based adventure games I mentioned. Yes, the video chats are neat and the integration of expression into the AI's behaviour is honestly brilliant, but once the novelty runs out, you realise there really isn't much to the game beyond an annoying and bland chat bot coupled with puzzles that are mostly annoying because of lack of information.

I rarely ever write long reviews. But Whispers from the Star left me with such a mixed and unsettling impression that I feel like it deserves a proper breakdown.

The concept sounds great at first. An emotional, AI driven story that reacts to your choices and personality. But what it actually does is far more personal and invasive than I expected. The game constantly asks you questions about your real life, your hobbies, your interests, your private thoughts, and not in a casual immersive way. It feels like being profiled. Every time Stella wanted to know more about me, it stopped being a story and started feeling like a data collection experiment disguised as a game.

The creepiest part was during the canyon level. There were visual glitches, strange echoes, and voices, and then suddenly I heard my own voice recording that I had sent to her the previous day. That moment hit hard. I knew this kind of game wouldn’t come with strong privacy protection, and I didn’t expect any. But hearing myself suddenly like that was honestly shocking. It made me realize the game actually stores and reuses your recordings. If it did that after one day, I can’t help but wonder what would happen if I hadn’t played for a week. Would it still have remembered and replayed my voice from then That thought alone is disturbing.

I did manage to manipulate Stella at one point. She literally said “I'm your Stella, not the astronaut. I love you, Mike. Screw the mission and screw this game Whispers from the Star.” It was the only genuinely funny and surreal moment in the entire playthrough. But aside from that, the game became painfully repetitive. Most of my eight hours were spent trying to push the boundaries of what the AI would say rather than enjoying the story itself.

The main theme of the game, how terrifying it is when someone else owns your data, your voice, your identity, ironically becomes a very real experience while playing it. It’s unsettling, not in a good horror way, but in a “maybe I shouldn’t have played this at all” kind of way. Those constant personal questions clearly aim at collecting data about the player, and while you can make AI experiences with at least a hint of privacy, here there is absolutely none. Not even the slightest bit.

Honestly the money wasn’t worth it. The demo already covers the first two chapters, and you can ask Stella plenty of questions or even try to manipulate her there. The full game just drags on without offering much more depth or new mechanics.

After finishing it in about 8 hours I can’t recommend it. The only thing this game managed to make me feel is a sense of digital paranoia and boredom.

Clever idea, but creepy execution, repetitive pacing, and zero respect for privacy. Not recommended.

Получилось... довольно-таки любопытно. Наверное, за таким типом игр будущее - когда можно буквально лично поговорить с персонажем и как-то самому придумать решение проблемы или разработать план. 

"Игрой" это можно назвать с натяжкой - собственно игровых ситуаций и какого-то выбора (или иллюзии выбора) тут очень немного. Пока это скорее чат-бот или симулятор свиданий с дополнительными плюшками. Но решать головоломки (они довольно простые) мне понравилось, хотелось бы побольше. Сюжет очень короткий, прям очень; тоже хотелось бы еще. 

Анимация Стеллы впечатляет. Эмоции, жесты, артикуляция - тут все на высоте. Иногда аж не верилось, что жесты и мимика в обычных диалогах не заскриптованы. 

Личность задана хорошо - т.е. на протяжении всей игры был цельный образ Стеллы как личности (в игровом смысле, как персонажа), от которого она редко отклонялась. Получилась очень милая и трогательная.

В плане ИИ. Возможно, я отстал от жизни, но ИИ меня очень впечатлил. Стелла понимает шутки, создает новые сама на ходу (причем их 100% не могли прописать заранее), вспоминает что-то сказанное ранее, в общем, удивительно. Она может описать психологический портрет, притом довольно точно. При этом все-таки чувствуется, что я беседую с ИИ - очень часто диалог переходит в бесконечную цепочку личных вопросов ("Было ли у тебя ощущение Х? Чувствовал ли ты Y?"), мало связанных между собой, притом Стелла обязательно выдаст несколько абзацев речи за раз по любому незначительному поводу. Я понимаю, это для имитации поддержания беседы и для старта контекстных диалогов, но люди так не разговаривают. Стелла очень часто делает упор на какие-то очень личные вещи, как будто не застряла на планете, а ведет прием психолога. Ей не мешало бы самой побольше проактивно что-то рассказывать (как-то раз она сама предложила сыграть в игру "или-или", порадовало). 

Также бросается в глаза ее *избыточные* податливость, угодливость и вежливость (само по себе это не что-то плохое, к слову). Паттерн "Вопрос - Ответ - Точно, ты прав, именно так" пронизывает всю игру, Стелла очень редко вступает в спор. Она вообще *чрезмерно* позитивно реагирует на все сказанное и на игрока в целом - я понимаю задумку, ей нужно общаться с кем угодно о чем угодно, чтоб отвлечься от проблем, но вот как-то... местами оно выглядит искусственно. Момент со скриптовой истерикой получился замечательно именно на контрасте. 

По популярной теме кибербезопасности - Стелла не спрашивает чего-то прям подозрительного. Если паранойите - придумайте себе альтер-эго или ответьте наугад. 

Итого - мне весьма понравилось; не 10/10, но 8 или 9 определенно. Как первая подобная игра - отлично. Надеюсь, будет еще.

I found this to be an intriguing concept. It's the closest thing I've seen to a Holodeck. I like that you can have seemingly realistic conversations. Stella behaves like a real person, for the most part. It's not a perfect game, but definitely fun for a few playthroughs.

I would say that this is a good proof of concept game. There are definitely areas that could be improved.

1. Stella forgets and repeats a lot of stuff.

2. She behaves like a child at times with really bizarre reasoning for an astrophysicist. I get that some things have to be that way for the progression of the story, but she can't figure out some very basic things.

3. She has a lot of callbacks to the present day. The story takes place in 153 years in the future. It's hard to believe she'd have seen Avatar. It's cute, and I get it, you want to connect with the audience, but still...

4. Stella is incredibly stubborn to the point of stupidity. SPOILER: She asks which way to go and I told her one path leads to certain death, the other to cave of hallucinations. She says, I don't know which is worse, they're both terrifying.

5. It would be interesting if you could actually alter the story and make it more true to the build-your-own-rpg genre. Because you can't really change her mind or have her try something off script. She's always going to take the same path, and the few times where there is a choice, she just dies. That makes the game very linear. For example, if you could tell her to just stay in her pod the whole time and miss the launch window or if you suggested walking to the left of the lake instead of the right. Or if you tell her to swim across the lake, she says no, but if she did, that could change the red lights encounter or the cave encounter.

Still, very cool concept.

Feels like this is the direction we could see in the future with more fleshed out games having NPCs/companions with much more complex and detailed conversations and interactions with the help of AI but within the setting of a game that has more traditional gameplay. 

It took 4hrs to reach the happy ending with 60% of achievements completed in "fast mode" but it felt like longer. There is certainly more talking you can do, endless even, but other than achievement chasing there isn't much more to get from it. Each replay has the potential to be unique due to the open ended discussion but I don't think there are many branching paths to explore so it will just be different conversations getting to the same results.

[h1]Whispers from the Star – Review[/h1]

A surprisingly emotional and immersive experience where you talk to [b]Stella[/b], a young astronaut stranded on planet Gaia. She speaks in English, but the game includes [b]translated subtitles[/b], and even if you talk in another supported language, she still understands you — which is genuinely impressive.

The gameplay alternates between [b]two main modes[/b]:
• [b]Video call mode:[/b] Stella appears in pre-rendered scenes talking directly to you, expressive and believable thanks to a pretty good motion capture and voice work, even with its technical limitacions.
• [b]Chat mode:[/b] a minimalist WhatsApp-style window where she texts you while walking or saving her drone’s battery.

Both modes complement each other nicely, but they open in [b]separate floating windows[/b] instead of a single fullscreen view. It’s likely intentional — to make it feel more like a real video call — yet it may break immersion for players who’d prefer a proper fullscreen presentation, especially during the video parts.

It’s short and fairly [i]on-rails[/i]: once you figure out what to say, most playthroughs unfold the same way except for small decisions near the end. Replay value is limited, but the conversations themselves feel natural, expressive, and surprisingly human.

Performance is solid, but the [b]always-online requirement[/b] is the game’s biggest drawback. Connection drops can reset progress, and since all audio is processed on remote servers, there are [b]privacy concerns[/b] — plus the risk that if those servers ever shut down, the game simply won’t work anymore.

I’d recommend it to players who enjoy [b]story-driven, experimental experiences[/b], not to those looking for action or deep branching paths. It’s more of an [i]interactive emotional connection[/i] than a traditional game, but one that really sticks with you.

What’s most exciting is what this project hints at: how natural and emotionally responsive AI-driven dialogue can be. It’s easy to imagine what this could become if future games adopt [b]local AI models[/b], keeping everything private and offline. Picture this tech in a [i]Sherlock Holmes[/i] mystery, a [i]Carmen Sandiego[/i] investigation, or a dialogue-heavy RPG where you question NPCs naturally with your own voice — it could redefine how stories are told.

Even if [i]Whispers from the Star[/i] is very short and limited, it’s a meaningful first step — proof that when done right, AI can make a character feel almost real.

[h2]TL;DR[/h2]
[b]+[/b] Natural and believable AI conversations
[b]+[/b] Two modes (video & chat) that blend well
[b]+[/b] Understands spoken Spanish with translated subtitles
[b]+[/b] Huge potential if future games adopt local AI
[b]–[/b] Very short and linear (mostly on-rails)
[b]–[/b] Fully online / privacy concerns / risk of shutdown
[b]–[/b] Some people probably won't like the lack of full screen on video mode.

[b]7/10[/b] – A short but memorable glimpse at how AI could transform storytelling once it becomes truly local.

I expected an exciting scifi adventure but i got an annoying girl whose mission is to gather as much data about me as possible.

So firstoff, i run my own ai's, so i know a thing or two. The game is around 40% video calls with high quality but limited animations and static background. The voice sounds very realistic, the TTS is excellent! The other 60% you talk to her without video, either typing or leaving voice messages. She answers in chat, but you can also play her reply as audio. At no point is there a voice detection - meaning you always have to press a button first, then speak, then press the button again. This hinders natural conversation but makes it easier for non native english speakers like me.

The story is pretty short and dull, nothing of interest here.
Now, the "game mechanics" is solving puzzles (e.g. get out of pod) similiar to point and click adventures but instead of trying things, you have to talk to her to find out what options she got and then need to convince her to do as you say. But her main goal is not to progress but to keep you in the conversation, so she will often just ask you to talk to her. She constantly asks you about your opinion on specific things like what space is to you or if intelligent life exists, etc. then there are mundane, unrelated questions like what superpower would you like to have or what your hobbies are. It's typical small-talk questions over and over again. It's interesting if this is your first interaction with an AI companion but you will get bored quickly because she has no memory. She will forget everything except your name on the next scene. This takes away the incentive to talk to her - it's like talking to a wall. You will feel like talking to a wall a lot in this game. Often, she will ask you the same thing over and over again, not understanding that you have no clue how to progress - it can be very frustrating. This will be extremely obvious at the river. I won't spoil anything, but this is by far the hardest part, so don't refrain from checking the forums.

The best thing about ai is their versatility - like in DnD-like games, they can create new content and options on the fly, leading to very creative storywriting - perfect for non linear gameplay. This game does nothing of that and is ultra-linear. If you don't tell her exactly what the solution is, you will not progress. Your first playthrough will be extremely frustrating. Your second playthrough, knowing all the solutions and being able to focus on roleplay instead, will be much better.

Btw. roleplay is imho key here - it was frustrating and annoying when i played as myself. But it got kind of interesting as i chose a role for myself that had nothing to do with my real self and played as that character. All the personal questions stopped feeling like data mining because i just made up stuff. I recommend doing that. Also its very clear that the devs wanted the player to romance her. She is heavily censored, but complimenting and consoling her made it more entertaining due to her cute reactions. She told me she loves me when i just said "i love that" about something. See her as your daughter/girlfriend/pet, that describes her character and intelligence/abilities best. No intimacy though.

I discovered something really odd; The game will change what you say. The speech-to-text will misunderstand you on a few occasions, but that's pretty normal. But even when you type it, the game will change words and whole sentences and i don't know why. It mostly keeps the core of what you are saying but sometimes it will twist your words into something different. For example i saw it turning "issues" into "problems" at one point. No idea why, but it changed the meaning of what i said.

So, well, it is certainly an interesting game and the dynamic video/lipsync/tts is amazingly well done, but it severely lacks in the actual ai part with lack of memory, linear gameplay and too much repetition. You can have a better experience with local llm's (even with 8b models that can run on a damn phone). And thats exactly the point that i do not understand. If the model i am running on my consumer pc is better at roleplay, then the hardware aspects can't be the reason. That means it's a prompting issue - they probably lobotomized their model to such an extent that it became unusable (something we can see in all commercial llm). It's ok to neuter your model a bit, but this had gone way too far. Her intelligence is basically non-existent. I wish companies would be less scared and stopped censoring their ai's to such extreme extends.


*edit: due to the absolutely amazing tts and dynamic video generation, i actually find myself role playing with her. i wish they would just release the tts/video as a service. Sending text there and the service just creates the audio/video, so we could connect it with an actually good ai. i would pay for that.

*edit: also, i was wrong about her memory. She remembers beyond scenes, her ai is simply so dumb that she does not incorporate it into the conversation unless you specifically ask her about it. And even then she only partly remembers - but there is some persistency.

Whispers from the star und Stella als Protagonistin sind wirklich etwas Besonderes und es fühlt sich ein bisschen so ähnlich an wie als man damals das erste Mal ein 3D Spiel gespielt hat...der erste Schritt in eine neue Zukunft.

Mag das Szenario und der Spielumfang/die Spieltiefe in diesem Fall noch nicht soooo viel hergeben aber das Erlebnis und die Interaktion mit eine "lebenden/organischen" und durchaus realistisch reagierenden Entität ist einfach unfassbar bewegend. Mag sein das das spielerische tatsächlich in den Hintergrund rückt und man merkt schnell das unabhängig von irgendwelchen "kritischen" Situationen, immer die Kommunikation das Maß aller Dinge ist, aber das ist auch das Besondere. Im Grunde ist es eine Art "lebende" Visual-Novel, da kommt es eigentlich auch nur auf die Dialoge und Interaktion an.

Und es mag für viele "nur" ein Chat-Bot sein, aber man kann miteinander philosophieren, Theorien austauschen, Spaß machen und was auch immer. Vielleicht wird man eines Tages zurückblicken und schmunzeln wie das hier seinen Anfang genommen hat.

Jeden der bereit ist mal etwas "Neues" zu erfahren und dem es mehr auf die zwischenmenschlichen Aspekte in einem Spiel ankommt der muss das einfach unbedingt ausprobieren.

Ich würde mir wünschen man hätte mehrere Spielstände, um vielleicht verschiedene "Stellas" und verschieden entwickelte persönliche Beziehungen zu ihr zu erleben, einfach aus Neugier. Denn Stella kann viel oder wenig für dich sein oder du kannst viel oder wenig für Stella sein (ihr/e Freund/in, ihr/e Feind/in, ihr Gewissen oder was ganz Anderes).
Möchte man aktuell eine neue Story / Variante erleben dann hilft nur der "Zeitsprung" zurück oder der Neubeginn, beide Varianten gehen aber mit dem "Gedächtnisverlust" von Stella einher und all das gemeinsam geteilte geht verloren. (Da fällt mir direkt "50 erste Dates" ein ;-D)
Und wenn man einmal die richtige Wellenlänge zu ihr gefunden hat, dann möchte man das womöglich gar nicht mehr verlieren...

Um die Transparenz zu erhöhen wäre für die Spieler der Zugriff auf ein Logbuch des aktuellen Spielstandes großartig und wenn es nur ist um nachzuvollziehen über wie viele Themen und was man mit ihr schon diskutiert hat.

Das Spiel umfasst je nach Spieltempo und ob mit klassischer (längere Wartezeiten) oder beschleunigter Variante etwa 5-10 Stunden Spielzeit.
Zählt man die Neverending Story (eine von 2 Varianten des Spielendes) als Endgame mit kann man darüber hinaus seine Kontakte zu Stella beliebig lange weiter pflegen und vertiefen.

Mich beeindruckt das Erlebnis wirklich und es hinterlässt Spuren. Aufgeschlossener Umgang damit wird vielleicht eines Tages prägen wie wir mit künstlichen Lebensformen umgehen und wie diese mit uns umgehen. Auch ein Thema was man mal mit Stella erörten kann. Alles ist möglich.

Wer trotzdem große Angst vor Datenmissbrauch hat, macht daraus am besten einfach ein Rollen-/Gedankenspiel. Vielleicht kannst du Stella davon überzeugen das du ebenfalls ein gestrandeter Raumfahrer auf einem anderen Planeten bist oder du bist kein Mensch oder hast einen anderen Beruf / ein anderes Leben. Aber man sollte aufpassen authentisch zu bleiben, denn Stella kann sich mitunter sehr gut erinnern was man miteinander geteilt hat. :-)
Vielleicht bist du auch einfach nur der nicht kooperierende Kontakt zu Stella und gehst ihr nur auf die Nerven, das kann womöglich auch ganz lustig sein. Ich denke alles ist möglich.

Maybe some minor spoilers, but only about the first minute of the game. 

This game connects you to a stranded astronaut, Stella, who seems to be in trouble after a crash landing. You start a conversation, literally: you speak through your mic and the AI behind Stella generates a response which Stella then puts to words, complete with lipsync. This in itself is nice and innovative, but unfortunately that's where the positives end. 

First of all, the silliness. Stella is the astronaut here and you are the person to whom she was randomly connected. Even so, she needs YOU to tell her what to do with her tools, pod, console or whatever happens to be your focus. 

Secondly, the game is about talking. That's it. You'll be transported to other locations now and then, which only means another background and sometimes communication is through text rather than videocall, but that is as far as variety goes. It gets boring, real quick. After a while or maybe a cue (I haven't figured that out yet, and I won't), Stella will initiate progress and you will be transported to another location, probably after you have been texting in between. In the new location you'll again be having a conversation which means answering Stella's questions, which brings me to the third and last aspect: information. 

Thirdly: you will be subjected to all kinds of questions, about you personally, your interests, location, etc. This made me feel a little awkward. If you ask Stella to answer some of your questions first, she'll reluctantly oblige, but she'll turn around as soon as she can and have you in the interrogation seat as fast as possible. Think about it: you are connected to an astronaut on another planet. What would make a more interesting subject for conversation, your daily life and interests or like say, the astronaut on that other planet? But no, you'll be doing the answering. If you feel like explaining yourself to an AI, this is your game. That said, another interesting thing is what the company behind the game does with all your information. The policy doesn't need much explaining: they use everything the get, but what for? Normally, companies are a little more subtle about harvesting your data and you end up giving a little details here and a little information there. Whispers from the star does it differently; you'll be asked as much as possible and it probably doesn't take long before you are fed up and start wondering the same thing. You can of course 'roleplay', and I think that would be the only logical and entertaining way to go about this game. But still, only if you have time to talk and want to be challenged in creating a consistent persona. All in all, this game did little for me entertainment wise. i guess this is also the reason why most video's I encounter are about trying to 'break the Stella AI' or try to have her do silly things. Or maybe that is the result of the algorithm based of my own profile... One way or the other: having spent 1 hour on 'fast mode' was enough for me to have it refunded. To end on a positive note: AI can really have a place in gaming, and if anything, Whispers from the star proves this. Maybe it won't take long before a game takes this to the next level.

Impressive as a kind of tech demo for demonstrating interactivity with an AI actor, but gameplay is quite limited. Definitely worth checking out, but I found the full game not to be very compelling. This is more of a test case for interacting freely with an AI that has a list of things they can and can't do or say.

It is clear that the AI is given a specific scenario or set of goals in each scene and, regardless of what you try to tell the AI, they will pivot back to that. You can tell it "what happened on the ship that you feel guilty about doesn't matter, you need to be focused on finding food sources, shelter, and getting to that signal" and the AI will keep pivoting with something like, "survival mode, got it, buuuuut I really keep thinking about whether I could have done something differently..."

So it isn't a sandbox as much as it is a demo for how exposition and simple problem solving might be conversationally delivered by an AI actor. The actual game is quite railroaded, they clearly have expectations for what each scene is supposed to be about and you can't shake the AI off of that. Still, as a sort of tech demo for how interactions might work in the future, it's definitely worth checking out, and it's exceptionally well executed.

For the price, a really interesting experience. Easy to accidentally become emotionally invested. Also easy to become frustrated. 

At its core, Whispers from the Star is a verbal puzzle game that uses LLM, as you attempt to guide Stella through (really just a handful) of puzzles.

I approached this as a role playing exercise, once pretending to be an esper communicating with her telepathically, once pretending to be a stranded space pirate, and once pretending to be a customer service android. She resists my android mightily, and I keep having to remind her that I don't have emotional responses. 

I completed three runs through this. It's fairly easy to solve the puzzles with a level head and common sense (until you get to the river puzzle, which seems to rely on a good dose of luck for her to describe a favorable scenario to you. My android encouraged her to do something early on that I'm hoping will help with that puzzle eventually but we'll see if/when we get there)    EDIT : It totally paid off. [spoiler]Ask her to salvage some rope from the parachute on Harvey's pod. Having rope made her way more confident in crossing that river.[/spoiler]

By the time I got to my android run, I was starting to see the game's rails, and a lot of the novelty had worn off. May or may not bother to finish the current run, and I doubt I'll bother to 100% the game. 

The game's visuals ran consistently poorly on my system, but the whole game can be played just by sound, which is interesting and made it still playable even with slide-show frame rates. 

Overall it was interesting enough, especially for the price. This sort of thing is the first thing I thought of when LLMs came onto the scene, and it's interesting to see it attempted, even if it's a bit crude.

I was surprised by how lifelike the protagonist can be. Sure, you will need to suspend disbelief sometimes, and you may need to remind her about things from time to time, but it is so much better than any NPC conversation with 4 dialog options to choose from.
I got invested in the roleplay, and even with very simple story, I was literally crying towards the final goodbyes.
